lessons.title: Oxy-Fuel Cutting
lessons.body: Oxy-fuel cutting uses a flame from burning fuel gas (acetylene, propane, or LPG) mixed with oxygen to heat steel to about 1,100Â°C, then a stream of pure oxygen burns the iron. It cuts mild steel from 3 mm to 300 mm thick. In Africa, LPG is common because acetylene is expensive and unstable in heat. You need a cutting torch, oxygen and fuel cylinders, regulators, hoses, and a spark lighter. Set oxygen pressure at 2â4 bar and fuel at 0.5â1 bar for 10 mm plate. Light the torch, adjust to a neutral flame (blue cone), preheat the edge until it glows orange, then press the oxygen lever and move steadily at 300â500 mm/min. Keep the tip 3â5 mm above the plate. For clean cuts, use a tip size matching thickness: a #1 tip for 3â6 mm, #2 for 6â12 mm, #3 for 12â25 mm. In dusty or windy sites, build a simple windbreak from corrugated sheets. Common mistakes: too much preheat (melts edges), too fast (incomplete cut), too slow (dross). Always wear goggles, gloves, and leather apron. In rural workshops, many use a 'cutting rig' made from a modified car alternator and a homemade torch; but safety first: never use petrol or improvised fuel. Oxy-fuel is ideal for thick sections, rusty steel, and demolition work where plasma is too expensive. Practice on scrap 10 mm plate: draw straight lines, circles, and bevels. After cutting, chip off dross with a chipping hammer and grind the edge if needed. Remember: oxygen is the cutting gas, fuel only preheats. Store cylinders upright, away from sun, and never oil fittings. With practice, you can achieve a cut quality good enough for welding without extra grinding.

lessons.title: Plasma Cutting
lessons.body: Plasma cutting uses an electric arc through a constricted gas (air, nitrogen, or argon) to create a plasma jet at 20,000Â°C that melts and blows away metal. It cuts mild steel, stainless, aluminium, and copper from 0.5 mm to 50 mm (handheld) or 150 mm (mechanised). In Africa, small inverter plasma cutters (e.g., 40A, 60A) running on 220V single-phase are popular. For a 40A machine, cut up to 10 mm mild steel at 400 mm/min; for 60A, up to 20 mm. You need a clean, dry air supply at 4â6 bar (use a filter-regulator). Connect the work clamp to bare metal. Set current: 30A for 3 mm, 40A for 6 mm, 60A for 12 mm. Hold the torch perpendicular, drag the tip on the plate (or use a standoff guide). Start the arc, then move steadily. Too fast leaves dross; too slow melts a wide kerf. For stainless, use nitrogen to avoid oxidation. In dusty environments, clean the torch tip daily. Common problems: worn consumables (electrode, nozzle) cause poor cut; moisture in air causes double-arcing. Replace consumables after 1â2 hours of cutting. Plasma is faster than oxy-fuel on thin plate (<20 mm) and cuts any conductive metal. It produces a narrow kerf (1â2 mm) and less heat distortion. Safety: wear shaded goggles (shade #5â8), keep away from flammables, and ensure good ventilation for fumes. Many workshops in Lagos or Nairobi use a 60A plasma cutter on a homemade CNC table for repeat parts. For field work, a generator of at least 7 kVA is needed. Practice on 6 mm plate: cut straight lines, then circles. Keep a spare set of consumables. With practice, plasma gives clean, weld-ready edges.

lessons.title: Shearing and Guillotine Cutting
lessons.body: Shearing cuts straight lines in sheet metal using a guillotine shear or a bench shear. A guillotine has a fixed lower blade and a moving upper blade that forces the metal down, creating a clean cut without chips. In Africa, manual foot-operated shears (up to 1.5 mm) and hydraulic shears (up to 6 mm) are common in fabrication shops. For a 3 mm mild steel sheet, a 2-metre manual shear costs about $800â$1,500. Set the back gauge to the desired width. Align the sheet against the side guide and hold it firmly. Step on the foot pedal or press the hydraulic button. The blade cuts from one side to the other. Keep hands clear of the blade. For thicker plate (6â12 mm), use a hydraulic shear with a hold-down to prevent slipping. Shearing produces a slightly deformed edge (rollover) but is fast and accurate for straight cuts. You can shear up to 3 mm on a manual machine; for 6 mm, you need a motorised shear. Common mistakes: cutting without clamping (sheet moves), dull blades (leaves burrs), and exceeding capacity (breaks machine). Always wear gloves. In many African workshops, a shear is used to cut blanks for doors, gates, and roofing sheets. For short cuts, a hand shear or nibbler works. Shearing is not for curves or thick plate. After shearing, deburr edges with a file or grinder. For production, set up a stop to repeat cuts. Maintain blades: sharpen or replace when they nick. A well-adjusted shear can cut 1,000 sheets before sharpening. Safety: never put fingers under the blade; use a hold-down. In rural areas, a simple lever shear mounted on a wooden bench can cut 1 mm sheet. Practice on 1 mm galvanised sheet: cut 100 mm strips. Check squareness with a try square. Shearing is the fastest way to cut straight edges in thin sheet.

lessons.title: Sawing and Abrasive Cutting
lessons.body: Sawing cuts metal with a toothed blade; abrasive cutting uses a high-speed disc that grinds through metal. For steel fabrication, common tools are hacksaws, portable band saws, chop saws (abrasive), and cold saws. A hacksaw with a 24 TPI blade cuts 25 mm round bar in about 2 minutes by hand. Use light pressure and let the blade cool. For faster work, a portable band saw (e.g., 1,000 W) cuts 100 mm pipe in 30 seconds. In Africa, a 355 mm abrasive chop saw (2,200 W) is common; it uses a 355 x 3 x 25.4 mm abrasive disc. For 50 mm square tube, a chop saw takes 10â15 seconds. Always wear a face shield, hearing protection, and gloves. Clamp the work securely. Let the saw reach full speed before cutting. Do not force the disc; let it cut. Abrasive discs wear down; replace when diameter drops below 250 mm. Cold saws (with coolant) cut cleaner and cooler but are expensive. For stainless, use a dedicated stainless blade to avoid contamination. In many workshops, a 'cut-off saw' with a petrol engine is used for on-site cutting of rebar and pipe. For accurate cuts, use a mitre guide. Common mistakes: using a worn disc (breaks), cutting without clamping (kickback), and wrong blade for material. For aluminium, use a blade with fewer teeth (10â14 TPI) and paraffin as lubricant. For thin sheet, use a fine-tooth blade (32 TPI). After cutting, deburr with a file. For large sections, a horizontal band saw with a coolant pump is ideal. In rural areas, a bow saw with a tungsten carbide blade can cut 50 mm steel. Always check the blade tension and alignment. Practice on 25 mm square tube: cut 10 pieces to length. Measure with a tape. Sawing and abrasive cutting are versatile but slower than shearing or plasma. Keep a spare disc or blade.

lessons.title: Laser and Waterjet Cutting
lessons.body: Laser cutting uses a focused beam of light to melt or vaporise metal; waterjet uses a high-pressure stream of water mixed with abrasive particles to erode metal. Both are computer-controlled (CNC) for high precision. In Africa, laser cutting is found in industrial hubs like Johannesburg, Lagos, and Nairobi; waterjet is rarer due to cost. A 1 kW fibre laser cuts 3 mm mild steel at 5 m/min, 6 mm at 2 m/min. It gives a kerf of 0.2 mm and a heat-affected zone of 0.1 mm. For stainless, use nitrogen assist gas. Waterjet cuts up to 100 mm steel with a 0.8 mm kerf, no heat distortion. A 4,000 bar pump with 0.3 mm abrasive (garnet) cuts 20 mm steel at 200 mm/min. Both need CAD files (DXF). For a small shop, outsourcing to a laser cutter costs about $2â$5 per metre for 3 mm steel. You cannot do laser or waterjet by hand; they are for repeat parts, intricate shapes, and thin sheet. In Africa, many fabricators send DXF files to a service centre. If you invest, a 1.5 kW laser with a 1.5 x 3 m bed costs $50,000â$100,000. Waterjet starts at $80,000. For most workshops, it is better to use plasma or shearing for simple cuts. However, for architectural panels, signage, and machine parts, laser gives a clean edge needing no finishing. Safety: laser requires enclosure (Class 1), waterjet needs guarding against high-pressure stream. In dusty environments, maintain clean optics and water filters. Practice by designing a simple bracket in Inkscape or LibreCAD, then sending to a service. Learn to nest parts to reduce waste. Laser and waterjet are not for thick, rusty steel; they need clean, flat material. For a beginner, focus on plasma and oxy-fuel first, then outsource laser for precision jobs.

lessons.title: Cut Quality and Edge Preparation
lessons.body: Cut quality determines how much grinding and welding you need. Key terms: kerf (width of cut), dross (resolidified metal on bottom edge), drag (lines angled back), and heat-affected zone (HAZ). For oxy-fuel, a good cut has sharp top edges, minimal dross, and a drag of less than 10% of thickness. For plasma, dross should be easily chipped. For shearing, edges are clean but may have rollover. After any cutting, you must prepare the edge for welding: remove dross, slag, and rust. Use a chipping hammer, then a 115 mm angle grinder with a 4.5 inch grinding disc. For a 6 mm plate, grind a 30Â° bevel on one edge for a V-groove weld. For a butt weld, leave a 2 mm root gap. Clean 25 mm back from the edge with a wire brush. For stainless, use a dedicated stainless brush to avoid contamination. In Africa, many welders skip edge prep, causing porosity and weak welds. Always check squareness with a try square and straightness with a straight edge. For critical joints, use a file to remove 0.5 mm of HAZ. If you cut with oxy-fuel, the edge may have a hard layer; grind it off. For plasma, the edge is usually weldable after light grinding. For laser, edges are often ready to weld. For waterjet, edges are smooth but may have abrasive residue; wash with water. Measure cut quality: use a vernier caliper to check kerf width (should be 1â2 mm for plasma, 0.2 mm for laser). Check for dross by visual inspection. If dross is heavy, adjust speed, gas pressure, or consumables. For sheared edges, deburr with a file. Always wear gloves and goggles. In a workshop, set a standard: no dross, no rust, no paint within 50 mm of the weld. Practice on 10 mm plate: cut with oxy-fuel, then grind a bevel. Weld it and bend test. Good edge prep saves time and ensures strong welds. Remember: cutting is only half the job; preparation is the other half.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of oxygen in oxy-fuel cutting?
options: D) To create a shielding gas
quiz.explanation: Oxygen combines with heated iron to oxidize (burn) it, creating the cut.

quiz.q: Which fuel gas is commonly used in Africa for oxy-fuel cutting due to its lower cost and stability?
quiz.explanation: LPG is cheaper and safer to store than acetylene, making it popular in African workshops.

quiz.q: What is the correct tip size for cutting 10 mm mild steel with oxy-fuel?
quiz.explanation: A #2 tip is recommended for 6â12 mm steel thickness.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of too much preheat in oxy-fuel cutting?
options: B) Melting of the top edge
quiz.explanation: Excessive preheat melts the top edge, creating a rounded, poor-quality cut.

quiz.q: Which gas is commonly used as plasma gas for cutting stainless steel to avoid oxidation?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen provides an inert atmosphere that prevents oxidation on stainless steel.

quiz.q: What is the typical current setting for a plasma cutter cutting 6 mm mild steel?
quiz.explanation: 40 A is a common setting for 6 mm mild steel with a handheld plasma cutter.

quiz.q: What causes double-arcing in plasma cutting?
options: B) Moisture in the air supply
quiz.explanation: Moisture in the air supply can cause the arc to double-arc, damaging consumables.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness a 40A plasma cutter can typically cut?
quiz.explanation: A 40A plasma cutter can cut up to about 10 mm mild steel.

quiz.q: Which safety equipment is essential for plasma cutting?
quiz.explanation: Plasma cutting emits bright UV light, requiring shaded goggles (shade #5â8).

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of shearing over plasma cutting?
options: B) Faster for straight cuts in thin sheet
quiz.explanation: Shearing is fast for straight cuts and produces no heat distortion.

quiz.q: What is the typical capacity of a manual foot-operated guillotine shear?
quiz.explanation: Manual shears typically cut up to 1.5 mm mild steel.

quiz.q: What is a common defect when shearing without clamping the sheet?
options: C) The sheet moves, causing inaccurate cut
quiz.explanation: Without clamping, the sheet can shift, leading to a crooked or inaccurate cut.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for cutting 25 mm round bar by hand?
quiz.explanation: A hacksaw with a 24 TPI blade is suitable for manual cutting of 25 mm round bar.

quiz.q: What is the recommended blade for cutting aluminium with a chop saw?
quiz.explanation: A blade with 10â14 TPI and paraffin lubricant works well for aluminium.

quiz.q: When should you replace an abrasive disc on a chop saw?
options: B) When diameter drops below 250 mm
quiz.explanation: Abrasive discs become unsafe when worn down below 250 mm diameter.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of abrasive disc breakage?
quiz.explanation: Worn discs are weak and can shatter under load.

quiz.q: Which cutting process uses a focused beam of light?
quiz.explanation: Laser cutting uses a focused, high-energy light beam to melt metal.

quiz.q: What is the typical kerf width for laser cutting 3 mm steel?
quiz.explanation: Laser cutting produces a very narrow kerf, around 0.2 mm.

quiz.q: What abrasive material is commonly used in waterjet cutting?
quiz.explanation: Garnet is the most common abrasive for waterjet cutting due to its hardness and cost.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of waterjet cutting over laser?
quiz.explanation: Waterjet cutting is a cold process, so there is no heat-affected zone.

quiz.q: What file format is typically required for CNC laser or waterjet cutting?
quiz.explanation: DXF is the standard CAD file format for CNC cutting machines.

quiz.q: What is 'dross' in cutting?
options: A) The width of the cut
B) Resolidified metal on the bottom edge
D) The angle of the cut
quiz.explanation: Dross is molten metal that resolidifies on the underside of the cut.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bevel angle for a V-groove weld on 6 mm plate?
quiz.explanation: A 30Â° bevel on each edge creates a 60Â° included angle for a V-groove weld.

quiz.q: Why should you use a dedicated stainless brush for stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: Carbon steel brushes can contaminate stainless steel, causing rust.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a root gap in a butt weld?
quiz.explanation: A root gap allows the weld to penetrate through the full thickness.

quiz.q: What should you do after oxy-fuel cutting to prepare the edge for welding?
options: B) Grind off the hard layer
quiz.explanation: Oxy-fuel cutting leaves a hard, oxidized layer that must be ground off.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that leads to porosity in welds?
quiz.explanation: Dirt, rust, and dross on the edge cause porosity; proper edge prep is essential.

quiz.q: How far back from the weld edge should you clean with a wire brush?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning at least 25 mm back ensures no contaminants enter the weld.

quiz.q: What tool is used to check the squareness of a cut edge?
quiz.explanation: A try square is used to check that edges are at 90 degrees.

quiz.q: What is the heat-affected zone (HAZ)?
options: A) The area that is melted
B) The area that is heated but not melted
C) The area that is cooled
D) The area that is painted
quiz.explanation: The HAZ is the region where the metal's microstructure is altered by heat but not melted.
